title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.




Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.




After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.




The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.




The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.

title: Mada Masr to challenge constitutionality of media law in Lina Attalah’s first court hearing
content:
During the first session in Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah’s trial on Tuesday morning, her defense counsel is to petition the court for access to evidence in the case, including documentation held by media regulators regarding the applications for a license that the organization has repeatedly filed since 2018.




It will also challenge the constitutionality of articles in the law regulating the press, requesting that the case file be referred to the Supreme Constitutional Court or that the defense counsel be granted authorization to file its own case before the court.




Attalah is present at the New Cairo misdemeanor court to attend the first hearing in her trial on charges of establishing, managing and operating a website without a license, following her investigation by the Supreme State Security Prosecution on October 21.




Lawyers are also set to attend the New Cairo court session on behalf of the Journalists Syndicate, which said on Monday that it has submitted a formal memorandum to the Supreme Media Regulatory Council “regarding the crisis over Mada Masr’s license application and the legal action linked to it.”




The memo stresses that there were violations of due process in the administrative handling of Mada Masr’s licensing application, that Mada Masr was not notified of the decision and that the proper recourse is “a challenge before the administrative judiciary rather than criminal prosecution,” according to a statement issued on Monday evening by syndicate head Khaled al-Balshy, which Mada Masr reviewed.




The syndicate’s lawyers are to submit a legal memorandum to the court during the Tuesday session in support of Mada Masr, based on arguments laid out in their memo to the SMRC.




More broadly, the syndicate called for a review of the licensing rules, as stated by Balshy.




The Supreme State Security Prosecution referred Attalah to the court on Thursday, less than 24 hours after questioning her on charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news, with the latter accusation dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.




Lawyer Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr’s legal counsel, 

described 

the “haste” in the referral and its scheduling as “unjustified urgency,” given the absence of circumstances in the case that require rapid resolution.




During trial proceedings, the defense counsel will seek from the court full access to evidence in the case, including the facts of the licensing procedures and related notifications, details of the charges Attalah is accused of and the time period over which it is alleged that the crime took place.




The defense team is also set to ask the court to grant them access to the full case file and to request that the court access all documentation regarding Mada Masr’s licensing application held by the SMRC.




It will request that the original SMRC notification rejecting Mada Masr’s license, which was not delivered to the organization, be brought before the court. The defense counsel will challenge the claim that Attalah received notice of rejection decision, requesting proof of its receipt.




Mada Masr has applied on multiple occasions since 2018 for a license to operate, when a new law organizing the media and the press was 

passed

, resubmitting its application 2020 upon the issuance of its bylaws.




It received no response from the regulatory council at the time. Instead, Attalah was informed by prosecutors, during a separate interrogation she was summoned to in 2022, that the SMRC had rejected the organization’s license application. Mada Masr responded by filing a lawsuit challenging the council’s failure to notify it of its decision.




Mada Masr will submit a memorandum to the court challenging the constitutionality of Articles 6 and 105 of Law 180/2018 Regulating the Press, the Media and the SMRC, arguing that they violate seven articles of the 

Constitution

: 65, 70, 71, 92, 95, 96 and 211.




In light of this, the defense is asking that the court either suspend the case and refer it to the Supreme Constitutional Court or that it permit the lawyers to file a case before the constitutional court themselves to seek a ruling on whether the two articles of the media law are consistent with the constitutional provisions specified.




Article 6 of the media law states that “websites may not be established or managed in the Arab Republic of Egypt, nor may offices or branches of websites operating from outside the country be managed, except after obtaining a license from the supreme council in accordance with the rules and conditions it sets in this regard.” For a breach of that article, the council may take the prescribed measures, including license cancellation, suspension of website activity or blocking where there is no valid license. The article provides for the council’s licensing decisions to be challenged before the administrative court.




Article 105 sets out penalties for violating certain provisions of the same law: a fine of LE1 to LE3 million, along with the closure and confiscation of equipment and devices. In a repeat offense, the article says, both the minimum and maximum penalty are doubled.

Mada Masr to challenge constitutionality of media law in Lina Attalah’s first court hearing

author: Mada Masr
title: Parliament gives Sisi mandate to back Saudi Arabia militarily, opposition rejects ‘blank-check authorization’
content:
Parliament authorized President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to “take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, following coordination between the two countries, to defend its territory, sovereignty and holy sites against any external attacks,” 

according 

to a statement issued by House of Representatives Speaker Hesham Badawy.




Lawmakers in the House, who had gathered for the third-closed door session on the matter in proceedings that began over an hour later than planned, stood in order to vote in support of the authorization, with a majority of two-thirds casting their votes in favor.




Twelve lawmakers from the Egyptian Social Democratic Party, along with four other opposition MPs — Diaa Dawoud, Atef Maghawry, Ahmed Farghaly and Abdel Alim Dawoud — refused to endorse the mandate, remaining seated during the vote, according to two parliamentary sources who spoke separately to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity. Lawmakers from pro-government parties voted in favor, they added.




Riyadh has made no official public statement, neither on Sisi’s request for parliamentary authorization nor on Parliament’s approval of it. Badawy’s statement, however, used the phrase “following coordination between the two countries,” instead of “if we are asked to do so,” the phrase Sisi 

used 

when he asked for the mandate earlier this month.




Saudi daily Okaz 

used

 Badawy’s formulation in its commentary on the decision, which it said “comes within the framework of Egyptian-Saudi coordination on the security challenges facing the region.”




One of the parliamentary sources said that Badawy did not open any of the three sessions by reading out the proposed measure or the relevant constitutional provision, as is customary when Parliament considers a presidential decree, agreement or similar measure. Instead, he merely 

asked 

lawmakers to indicate their positions and vote on authorizing the president to take “defensive measures” to protect Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested them, he added.




The same source stressed that parliamentary custom requires that lawmakers be given specific details — not shared with the press — including the nature of any mission assigned to Egyptian military forces that are to operate abroad, the size and composition of the force and the mission’s duration. None of these details was presented during the sessions, the source said. Instead, Parliament only gave the president authority to act in coordination with Saudi Arabia, he added.




The Constitution requires parliamentary approval when troops are sent on a combat mission outside the borders, making it necessary to provide lawmakers with basic information about the mission, the source said. Granting the president “blank-check authorization,” the source argued, is a contentious issue.




Egyptian Social Democratic Party member Freddy al-Bayady likewise told Mada Masr that no details were presented in either of the two previous sessions, as well as in Monday’s, on the nature and limits of the military mission, the duration and scope of the authorization, its financial and human risk or the risk of the conflict widening and affecting Red Sea and Suez Canal navigation. 




Bayady holds a seat in the House, butunable to attend Monday’s session as he was out of the country, he told Mada Masr.




He stressed that his party’s MPs stand in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reject attacks on its territory, but need enough information to make a decision after weighing the consequences.




Egypt has previously provided military support to Saudi Arabia during Operation Decisive Storm in 2015, and to the United Arab Emirates earlier this year, without putting the matter before Parliament, the parliamentary source noted.




In their viewpoint, bringing the matter before Parliament this time indicates that the planned support could go beyond a limited deployment of equipment or troops, something that he argued compelled the state to seek out parliamentary approval this time.




Article 152 of the Constitution 

requires 

the president to consult the National Defense Council before declaring war or sending armed forces on combat missions outside the country. It also requires approval from two-thirds of the members of the House, voting in a closed session under Article 130 of the House’s bylaws.




In May, Egypt sent a “

detachment

” — a limited military formation drawn from one or several corps — to the UAE. Sources at the time said that the word “detachment” came to “signal the limited size of the formation and the limited duration of the presence,” a gesture of Egyptian support for the UAE against Iranian attacks that stopped short of real Egyptian involvement in the war.




Before that, Egypt had taken part in Operation Decisive Storm, the coalition that Saudi Arabia has led in Yemen since 2015. It 

dispatched 

four naval vessels to secure the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Gulf of Aden, alongside air force participation. Cairo 

said 

at the time that it is prepared to send ground troops “if the situation warrants,” but it never did.




On October 17, Sisi called for an emergency parliamentary session during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation ceremony, asking lawmakers to authorize him to take any measures necessary to protect Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks “if we are asked to do so.”




“We are not looking for a role to play, but it makes no sense whatsoever for us to allow any harm to come to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its security or its stability,” he said during the ceremony.




He appealed to “everyone in the Gulf” to stop the war. “Regardless of this appeal, whether it is heeded or not, Egypt, in line with His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman’s directives, will carry out any measure to protect and defend you,” he added.




The president stressed that he is not speaking “in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. We are speaking only in defense.”




After Sisi’s remarks, House Speaker Hesham Badawy called an emergency plenary session for the following morning. 




Before Parliament convened on October 18, the presidential spokesperson 

announced

 three points agreed upon by the National Defense Council at a meeting chaired by Sisi earlier that day. The council declared Egypt’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia, out of a belief that Saudi national security is tied to Egyptian and Arab national security, and pledged to provide the country with all necessary and available forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity and safeguard Islamic holy sites.




The council also called for continued and intensified political and diplomatic efforts, in coordination with relevant regional and international parties, to de-escalate tensions across the region and peacefully resolve the crisis affecting it.




Then, Parliament held a three-hour closed-door session before postponing a final decision. The vote was deferred to sessions scheduled for October 19 and 20. On October 19, however, lawmakers postponed the vote again until Monday, citing the need to give all MPs an opportunity to express their views.




As Parliament held its first session last week, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, Ahmed al-Tayeb, 

called 

for the urgent formation of a mediation committee comprising respected, wise figures from Arab and Muslim countries. The committee, he said, should work to halt armed conflicts across the region and bridge differences between the parties involved. He expressed his readiness to support its efforts but stopped short of explicitly opposing Egyptian military defense measures to protect Saudi Arabia.




In a new statement, Tayeb 

condemned

 on Monday morning the Houthi attacks on Mecca, Madinah and Saudi civilian infrastructure, calling for them to stop and renewed his appeal for the committee’s formation.




With Parliament’s decision still pending, Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty and General Intelligence Service chief Hassan Rashad 

traveled

 to Riyadh on October 21, where they met Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman and delivered a message from Sisi to King Salman bin Abdel Aziz. 

According 

to Abdel Atty, the message reaffirmed Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia in the face of the attacks while stressing the need to seek a political solution to the crisis.




Earlier that day, Sisi had also 

said 

that any Egyptian military support for Saudi Arabia would be aimed at protecting the kingdom’s territory and borders, not launching attacks on Yemen.




The Saudi-Houthi front is witnessing its most violent 

escalation 

since the collapse of the truce that had held since 2022.




On Monday, the Houthis 

said 

they attacked oil pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline and Riyadh airport. The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, announced that it destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, one of which it said had been used to fire a missile toward Riyadh.




According to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium published on Monday, around 86 percent of scheduled flights at King Khalid International Airport were canceled between October 8 and October 25.




In July, the Houthis declared a “naval blockade” of the kingdom and attacked Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. In September, they launched a ground attack, capturing the Yemeni Port of Mokha, which had been under the control of the Saudi-led coalition’s joint forces, effectively controlling Bab al-Mandab. By early October, the two sides were escalating: the internationally recognized Yemeni government launched the Fajr al-Yemen Operation to retake Sanaa, backed by extensive Saudi air support, while the Houthis attacked facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco and 

struck

 King Khalid International Airport, killing 12 people and wounding hundreds.

Parliament gives Sisi mandate to back Saudi Arabia militarily, opposition rejects ‘blank-check authorization’

author: Rana Mamdouh
title: St. Catherine Monastery’s land ownership lawsuits adjourned after archbishop backs Egypt-Greece deal
content:
St. Catherine’s Monastery’s archbishop said on Saturday that he intends to sign an agreement with the Egyptian government that would organize the religious community’s relationship to the monastery and surrounding lands where they have based their spiritual life for over 1,400 years.




Egypt’s government had put forward a draft proposal in July that would consolidate ownership of the monastery and surrounding lands in the hands of the Egyptian state for the first time, following decades of dispute over the status of the religious sanctuary in South Sinai, which has effectively been independent of state and legal frameworks, since its history at the site predates these frameworks’ jurisdiction.




The dispute had escalated when the Ismailia Court of Appeals 

issued

 a 2025 ruling establishing the state’s ownership of the monastery lands, granting the monastery’s usufruct rights to occupy and manage a majority of the property but ordering the expulsion of the monastery’s then-archbishop from a portion of the lands on the grounds that he had seized them unlawfully. The ruling precipitated a series of competing claims to the monastery and its lands and a crisis over the monastery’s leadership. Those competing claims are poised for resolution following the archbishop’s indication over the weekend that he would agree to the government’s proposal, although the former archbishop voiced condemnation for the agreement on Saturday, claiming the religious community is being pressured to accept.




With Symeon Papadopoulos, the archbishop of Sinai, Pharan and Raitho, 

stating

 that he intends to sign an agreement with the Egyptian government that would bring an end to the pending legal proceedings and disputes over the monastery’s status, a parallel legal process that sought to challenge the court ruling was postponed on Sunday by the Ismailia Court of Appeals.




While the 2025 ruling had upheld the government’s ownership of the monastery and surrounding lands, the court was still reviewing the monastery’s ongoing challenge to the ruling in favor of the case’s complainants: the South Sinai Governorate, the antiquities minister and the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency’s head.




The court, sitting in the Tor circuit and presided over by judge Alaa Abdel Razeq, nevertheless adjourned the cases until December 27, citing the need for the parties to establish in the case files the legal capacity of the person running the monastery’s affairs.




Papadopoulos has said he will arrange a date to sign the agreement with the monks and the Egyptian government “as soon as his health permits.”




The archbishop’s announcement was welcomed with relief from both the Egyptian and Greek governments.




In a statement published on Saturday, the Foreign Ministry 

said

 it had received a letter from Papadopoulos confirming he would sign the contract concerning the monastery and the surrounding lands “once a date for the [signing] ceremony is set.” The statement also said the agreement upholds the Ismailia Court of Appeals ruling “in full compliance with relevant national legislation, bringing all legal proceedings to an end.”




Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis, meanwhile, thanked Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty for what he described as their role in making the agreement possible. In a statement, Gerapetritis 

said 

the agreement “ensures, in perpetuity, the preservation of the Monastery’s religious character and that of its ecclesiastical properties, as well as the continuity of the Monastery through the granting of long-term residence permits to its monks.”




The monastery’s lawyer, Fathy Ragheb, however, told Mada Masr that legal proceedings are still pending before the Court of Cassation and the Court of Appeals, with no final rulings so far. Ragheb asked for more time to consult with officials responsible for the monastery before providing further comment on the fate of these cases.




Mada Masr also attempted to reach representatives of the monastery for comment but received no response as of time of publication.




Former Archbishop Damianos’s position stood in even starker contrast to the welcome from Egyptian and Greek state officials.




Damianos 

accused

 the Greek government, represented by the prime and foreign ministers, of exerting “unbearable” pressure on the monks in recent days to force them to sign what he described as a “shameful and unacceptable” settlement with the Egyptian state.




“I am sure that my brothers will not open the back door for the fall of our Holy Monastery,” he added.




Damianos also said that the Greek government circulated information that Egypt’s Court of Cassation could issue a final ruling  on Saturday in the monastery’s case, in a bid to pressure Papadopoulos and the monks into signing the agreement proposed by the Egyptian government.




Commenting on Papadopoulos’s stated intention to conclude the deal, Damianos said he was “saddened” by the decision, adding that the archbishop’s remarks neither disclosed the terms of the proposed settlement nor indicated that the other monks had consented to it, as required under the monastery’s statutes.




He stressed that Papadopoulos has no right to unilaterally sign any settlement that would entail relinquishing “centuries-old historical titles.”




Damianos’ 52-year leadership of the monastery came to an abrupt end in 2025. The conclusion of his leadership was precipitated by the Ismailia court ruling, which included orders to evict Damanios, in his capacity as the archbishop of St. Catherine’s Monastery at the time, from 14 disputed properties in the monastery compound in South Sinai on the grounds that he had seized the land without legal basis and carried out construction without official permits.




The former archbishop 

claimed

 on Saturday that he had established an out-of-court agreement with the Egyptian government, before the 2025 court ruling, that would have seen the government explicitly and unreservedly recognize the Holy Monastery of Sinai as owner of all 71 disputed properties. The agreement was never formally signed, he said, and instead, the Ismailia Court of Appeals emerged on May 28, 2025 to affirm the Egyptian government’s ownership of the monastery’s lands, granting the monastery usufruct rights only to 57 of the total 71 properties.




“The agreement was not signed because the Egyptian government, with which Mr. Gerapetritis was supposedly negotiating, allowed the decision of the Ismailia appeal court to be issued,” added Damanios.




“The issue is not only legal; it is primarily political,” he continued. “No one can hide behind the decisions of Egyptian ‘justice’ in order to evade their own responsibilities.”




Damanios’s response to the court ruling at the time, however, was to endorse a Greek draft law that would have handed sweeping control over the monastery’s assets to an Athens-based public authority.




The move prompted a dispute over his leadership, to which he responded by sending a private guard down to throw a number of monks out of the monastery in retaliation, drawing the Patriarchate’s intervention.




In a document compiled by the monks detailing their grievances and sent to Mada Masr at the time, they described Damianos’s move to locate the monastery’s assets under a legal framework in Greece without consulting them and obtaining the approval mandated by the monastery’s statutes as “the ultimate betrayal of the monastery” and a culmination of a longer breakdown in trust.




The monastery’s monks voted to depose Damianos and 

unanimously

 elected Papadopoulos in his place, though there were no other nominees. An informed source told Mada Masr at the time that figures in the Greek Orthodox Church had refused to grant rival candidates ecclesiastical release to put their names forward.




In July, the Egyptian government, represented by its foreign and justice ministers, 

presented 

Papadopoulos with a new agreement containing several provisions. Chief among them was recognition of the monastery as an Egyptian legal religious entity, granting the monks “religious possession” of the monastery and its religious institutions — meaning the right to reside on the grounds and practice religious rites — and allowing them to lease the surrounding gardens and land from the Egyptian government for a nominal fee over an extended period, a source close to the monastery 

told

 Mada Masr at the time on condition of anonymity.




Its abbot and monks, who hold Greek, American and Lebanese nationalities, would also be granted three-year, renewable residence permits, according to the source.




The foreign and justice ministers had met with Papadopoulos for more than seven hours in July, pushing him to agree to the deal in exchange for a presidential decree ratifying his election and appointment as the monastery’s head, the source said. Papadopoulos had been in a compromised position since his election in 2025, with no official recognition of his post issued by the Egyptian state, according to the source. This has left the archbishop unable to deal with the monastery’s Egyptian bank accounts or conduct transactions with state institutions in South Sinai.




The source noted that while Papadopoulos holds a Greek diplomatic passport, which allows him to travel to and from Egypt for two years, the rest of the monks hold 12-month tourist visas that take three months to renew, leaving them with, in reality, only nine months of residency.




The proposed arrangement would follow the precedent set by former President Anwar al-Sadat, who had appointed Damianos as archbishop and later granted him Egyptian citizenship.




The Egyptian government’s proposed agreement builds off the May 2025 Ismailia court 

ruling

, which recognized the state’s ownership of St. Catherine’s Monastery and its lands while granting the monks limited usufruct rights for religious use and possession. The ruling also placed all dealings involving the properties under the direct supervision of state authorities.




The court also ruled that the monastery’s spiritual affiliation with the Greek Orthodox Church does not confer any legal privileges on it within Egypt.




The Ismailia court split the disputed lands into four categories. The first covers the land on which the monastery itself is built, along with other plots that hold some churches and shrines. The monks and archbishop were granted what the court termed “religious possession” of these properties for residence and worship, while ownership remains with the state under the supervision of the Supreme Council of Antiquities.




The second category comprises lands outside the monastery’s boundaries, which the court incorporated into the St. Catherine Protectorate under the supervision of the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency.




The third consists of agricultural land that the court termed “expulsion lands,” ordering the monks be expelled from it on the grounds that they are occupying it by force.




The fourth includes several plots with small churches and monastic facilities covered by preliminary contracts between the monastery and the local administrative unit of St. Catherine. The court ruled that these contracts did not transfer ownership but instead established reciprocal obligations.




The source close to the monastery, as well as a second one, previously told Mada Masr Greece supports the Egyptian proposal, and Egyptian officials were working to pressure Papadopoulos and the rest of the monks to agree to the terms, despite what the sources said is a relinquishment of the monastery’s land ownership.




They also said  Egyptian government representatives put forward the new agreement in July after reaching an understanding with the Greek government.




The Friends of St. Catherine’s Monastery Facebook page, which reflects the views of a number of monks, 

described

 at the time the agreement as a disastrous formula that dismantles the monastery of its rights and deprives it of its ownership.




The group argued that the Egyptian and Greek governments were placing their political and economic interests above the spiritual and historical significance of one of the world’s oldest inhabited monasteries where religious rites are still held.




The monastery is being sold in the market of political and economic interests in exchange for the 

energy agreement

 that Athens seeks to conclude with Cairo, the group stated.




The 2025 court ruling established the state’s ownership of the area for the first time, leaving it at the mercy of the state, which can revoke its legal standing at any time, 

according

 to Stephan Dömpke, the head of World Heritage Watch, an independent organization dedicated to protecting UNESCO sites, who spoke to Mada Masr at the time of the court ruling.




“Being at the mercy of the Egyptian government is what terrifies the monastery and the whole Orthodox Church,” Dömpke told Mada Masr, “especially when considering the tourism developments unfolding around them without their consent.”




In 2021, the Egyptian government launched the “Great Transfiguration” 

project

, aimed at transforming the city of St. Catherine into an international center for Abrahamite religions. Since then, large-scale construction has taken place in the city and around the monastery as part of what the government has described as a “developmental and touristic” initiative.

St. Catherine Monastery’s land ownership lawsuits adjourned after archbishop backs Egypt-Greece deal

author: Mada Masr
title: Maybe, tomorrow
content:
On a good week, our job feels like the ideal job. You don’t need to wrestle with making sense of the big picture and then pull a break to focus on your own life. Your life is all about trying to make sense with and for everyone around you, and to do so, you summon your tools, nourish them, sharpen them. These include looking for the facts, especially the hidden ones. You sift through material, you speak to sources, you go back to the material in ongoing loops. You need the history to draw the context. It changes all understanding of facts. You need the social sciences to read the data critically. You need the aesthetics of form to weave the story and start journeying it to the public. You need some philosophy for the whole thing to come together, because there is just a lot of paradox. You are also tempering a little with time, because understanding might instruct a thing or two for tomorrow. 




Isn’t one fortunate, theoretically speaking, to be a journalist? We know you might not agree with us.




This past week would have been an ideal one for all the above. First, the president announced, for the first time in Egyptian modern history, what was widely read as a serious intention for a transition of power by the end of this term. This is while a multilayered war continues to change the shape of the region, 

with Egypt’s looming intervention

. And back at home, as part of the domestic power calculus, a six-day forum was rolling on broadcast to showcase the government’s achievements in the last years. In the background, the Egyptian pound kept losing value and now the dollar crossed an unprecedented LE55 mark. 




Throughout this week, we 

raised our questions

 about the president’s plans and published a 

podcast

 reflecting on the different possibilities of this shift in mode of rule, but, also, what is it that we should be doing now, as political subjects, in the wait? What does waiting politically look like? In our investigative work, we get to inhabit a common triumphalist moment in journalism where hard questions are answered and the answer is usually difficult to get, shocking to receive, scandalizing for those in power. But on some days, when we don’t have the answers, as in a significant moment where the president is speaking about power transfer and a shift in the mode of rule, we don’t shy away from asking questions and publishing them. It’s a moment where journalism embeds itself more tightly with the people it is rooted in, collectively wondering: what’s next? 




This past week, we also published this 

piece

 about the return of some families to their villages occupied by Israel in South Lebanon in the recent war. We have been looking into the region, not from the standpoint of a regional media, but more out of a sense of urgency to record where drastic change is unfolding, whether as tangible reality on the ground, or as ideation by those in power from their closed rooms. We have expanded in different directions because that’s a way to make sense of what’s happening. On the same day, we published our weekly 

Palestine bulletin

, a bulletin that started with the genocide in 2023, where we keep reporting about Gaza and Palestine as a whole, even after a ceasefire inked on a paper was sold to the world as the end of the war. On the weekend, we published the weekly 

Sudan bulletin

, a space that has been gathering developments on the ground and on power politics, highlighting why it is important not to sever Sudan from the regional calculus. 




In the same week, we joined an initiative of a collective newsroom made up of eight independent media in the region, to fill up the silenced space of Matsda2sh, the fact-checking platform whose entire newsroom of six journalists were arrested last month. Together with the other organizations, we worked on fact-checking information presented at the aforementioned government forum. 




To this date, our colleagues in Matsda2sh are still being held in remand detention. Some reported being subjected to mistreatment, and all of them shared with their families upon first prison visits the feeling that they are enclosed in a nightmare that has no end. 




We have worked with some of the six journalists before they moved on to Matsda2sh; we knew them as young, aspiring journalists wanting to genuinely learn how to understand what is happening around us and how to communicate a record of this understanding to the broader public. Before it became a nightmare, they also thought journalism could be an ideal job, especially in tumultuous times.  




We are going to court on Tuesday on accusations that we are an illegal entity. It is an interruption through which we repeat our own version of the story uttered against us time and again, dancing with absurdity time and again: We are a legal entity because we are always seeking to be legal, we are defending the law against its constant recoil as a tool of power, so much so that it is risking losing itself to total nullity, a crisis for the whole country. We are not just fighting for ourselves, but to re-expand the law as it should be, to be a space through which we can operate, a space in which our colleagues in Matsda2sh and every other journalist in custody can be free. The real threat to those in power, before it being a threat to us, is the entire removal of that space.




We understand that interruptions and disruptions are normal parts of this ideal job of journalism, when it entails making sense against the grain of power, power that thinks of itself as consolidated, locked, comfortable. The trick is always in how to absorb the rupture and return, how to delay the end if an end has to be imposed upon you, how to keep today going, on our terms, perhaps tomorrow too. This is perhaps how we learned to wait in the dark, in times of crisis, to be active in the waiting, regardless of that which we are fearing the wait for.




We understand that a sword will most likely be raised above our heads very soon. Even the faintest spark shakes darkness to the grounds. We still think of all of this as an interruption, because that’s how you fight a political fight. You remember that time is not linear, ends are not pre-written. You are powered by the uncertainty of the maybe.




And so, in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday. 




And we are open to receiving love letters in the middle.




There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism. Put together, they point to the collective that springs out in a moment of danger. It’s a community of our imagining that comes down tangibly, a journalism receiving its feedback loop, a people united in their desire to know, to think together and to defend and protect that space from closure.




We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small 

us

, Mada Masr, but a much bigger 

we.

  

The post 

Maybe, tomorrow

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Mada Masr
title: Organizations rally in support of Mada Masr, condemn ‘weaponization’ of media law against independent journalism
content:
Rallying in support of Mada Masr, statements of solidarity have emerged in recent days from domestic and international advocacy organizations, political figures and parties, journalists and media platforms, all expressing their backing for the independent journalistic website and for Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah, following her referral to trial last week by prosecutors.




Though Mada Masr has been called in for questioning on an almost annual basis in relation to journalistic coverage, this is the first time prosecutors initiate a trial of this kind. Attalah is due to attend a misdemeanor court session in New Cairo on Tuesday on the charges of founding, managing and operating a website without a license.




During a gathering at the Journalists Syndicate on Saturday, several General Assembly members and independent journalists declared their support for Mada Masr and condemned what they described as an “assault on independent journalism,” referring to the escalation that began in September with the arrest of six journalists from the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh.




In the ensuing weeks, Attalah received a summons for investigation, 

fielding

 six hours of questioning from the Supreme State Security Prosecution about her efforts to acquire a license for Mada Masr since 2018, the website’s operations, as well as questions concerning a recent report on protest actions taken by prisoners across the country and authorities’ response.




She was informed less than 24 hours after the investigation session that she has been referred to trial on charges of running an unlicensed website.




Following news of the trial referral, 119 human rights organizations and media institutions from around the world came together to condemn the “unprecedented attack on press freedom in Egypt,” in a Friday 

statement

 calling for an end to the legal pursuit of Attalah and urging that Mada Masr be granted a license to operate following its multiple applications to media regulators.




They also called for Egypt’s authorities to halt the targeting of independent media outlets — including Matsda2sh — and to release all 26 journalists currently imprisoned in Egypt in relation to their work.




The list of signatories to the joint statement includes Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, the Committee to Protect Journalists, PEN International, the International Federation for Human Rights, the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Center and the Electronic Frontier Foundation.




Also among the signatories are the International Fact-Checking Network, the Center for International Policy, the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy and dozens more Arab and international media platforms.




The signatories stated that Attalah’s trial threatens the future of independent journalism, knowledge production and civil society in Egypt. They warned that the potential penalties — fines ranging from LE1 to LE3 million and possible orders for the website’s closure — could effectively end the operations of one of the last remaining independent media institutions in the country.




Individual expressions of support were also forthcoming from Democratic United States’ Senator Chris Van Hollen, who called the charges against Attalah “baseless,” and described the events from Matsda2sh’s arrest to Attalah’s pursuit as “the most severe crackdown on the press seen in years.”




Van Hollen, a member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, called for an end to the assault.




Amnesty International had already demanded on Wednesday an end to what it described as the persistent judicial harassment of Attalah and Mada Masr’s journalists, prior to the trial referral, with Yasmin Ahmed, the organization’s regional impact director, stating that targeting the editor-in-chief for the journalistic work produced by her team is “outrageous” and pointing to the fact that this is the sixth case brought against the outlet and its journalists in the span of six years.




The Committee to Protect Journalists’ regional director, Sara Qudah, likewise 

described

 these recent actions as a coordinated assault on the press, condemning Attalah’s referral to trial “for operating a website without a license that Egyptian authorities have themselves refused to grant for years.”




Lawyer Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr’s legal counsel, stressed in comments on Thursday that the outlet has been seeking a license since 2018, following the issuance of the law regulating the press and the media.




Once the executive regulations were issued two years later, Mada Masr resubmitted its application. On both occasions it received no response.




It was only during another summons for questioning in 2022, in relation to a 

report

 at the time, that Attalah was informed by prosecutors that the media regulator had rejected the outlet’s application.




With no information about the rejection nor the Supreme Media Regulatory Council’s grounds for refusing to issue the license, Mada Masr challenged the council’s failure to notify it of its decision before the administrative courts in 2022, learning through the course of legal proceedings, a year later, that the SMRC had deemed its application to be incomplete.




It accordingly submitted the additional documentation, as part of another round of application that has remained pending since 2023, with no response to date.




“Egypt is weaponizing its media law to punish independent journalism and intensify one of its worst crackdowns on the press in years,” said CPJ in its statement of support.




As well as the international voices condemning the move against independent journalism, political forces and media organizations inside Egypt have expressed their support for Mada Masr and their concern about the future trajectory of domestic media.




The Civil Democratic Movement 

condemned

 Attalah’s prosecution and the restrictions placed on independent media outlets, describing the SMRC as a tool acting to stifle Mada Masr and other press institutions by withholding licenses or neglecting to respond to their applications.




The movement pointed to the uncomfortable juxtaposition of the government’s Egypt Forum 2026, showcasing its political achievements, and the ongoing pursuit of journalistic platforms offering critical perspectives on public policy.




“Freedom of the press and a plurality of voices are not a threat but are prerequisites for any serious political reform,” the movement stated.




The Bread and Freedom Party also 

announced

 its solidarity with Mada Masr and Matsda2sh’s journalists, calling on the media council to process pending license applications and halt measures that threaten to close independent media outlets. The party further urged an expansion of professional syndicate protections to include journalists working for websites and digital platforms.




Attalah is due to attend trial on Tuesday, October 27.

The post 

Organizations rally in support of Mada Masr, condemn ‘weaponization’ of media law against independent journalism

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.
