title: Khartoum courts UN-backed relief to stave off truce pressure; Tasis govt heedful after health minister’s angry exit; Abyei strike tests Juba ties; Drones hit RSF, military’s seats of power; RSF pushes in Kurmuk, military wins Geisan ground
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

 

here

.




From Khartoum and Nyala, to a gold mine in South Kordofan, a town in West Kordofan and a power station in White Nile, drones tore through Sudan this week, killing hundreds and destroying homes, livelihoods and critical infrastructure.




Both sides traded blame, and each pointed to neighbors it said let the drones through. Some strikes went unclaimed, but silence from the military over its attack on the disputed Abyei region didn’t stop Juba from summoning Sudan’s ambassador on the same day to warn of a “dangerous development” in a border territory already straining relations between the two countries. Khartoum weighed in days later, with a Foreign Ministry statement denying the military was involved.




The strike on the RSF-held Naam market in Abyei set fuel depots burning. The fires were still consuming the area as the death toll exceeded 150 and thousands were displaced, and residents took to the streets in protest, activists and Abyei administration sources said.




In the Security Council, in Geneva and among mediators on Sudan, the warnings this week over the drone war and the humanitarian toll sounded much as they have for months, and they still amount to little beyond adding pressure on the warring parties to stop the fighting.




But Khartoum won’t concede an end to 

RSF territorial control 

before a truce can take hold, and won’t see the paramilitary group at the table in any political process on the country’s future.

 

So instead of committing to a broader settlement, it is now trying to show it can deliver on humanitarian issues, betting that progress on aid deliveries and civilian protection will 

blunt

 international criticism, former and current Sudanese officials and sources close to the Transitional Sovereignty Council told Mada Masr.




Hence the letters to Western capitals over the week and the talks with the United Nations on internationally monitored aid deliveries, which allow Khartoum to appear willing to engage without participating on terms it rejects, former officials said. Any plan, however, has to keep aid under the authority of state institutions, they added.




In western Sudan, the RSF’s parallel administration is trying to hold on to the very recognition Khartoum is trying to deny it, but its own infighting is getting in the way. Tasis’s Cabinet is trying to take oversight of medical aid away from a health minister who had protested for months over interference by the RSF and influential figures looking to monopolize medical supplies. He left for Nairobi in protest last week, and a government already reeling from recent defections is treading carefully, wary of another exit that would further damage its image as a viable administration before aid organizations.




In Blue Nile State, the push and pull on the battlefield goes on. The RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, tried to take two of the military’s bases in Kurmuk locality, part of the network protecting the state capital of Damazin, though accounts of how it ended conflict. The military, meanwhile, gained ground in neighboring Geisan locality, taking two areas that a former military officer said could help check the RSF’s new advances in Wad al-Mahi locality.




***




Military drone strike on Abyei market draws protest from Juba




Caption: Undersecretary of the South Sudanese Foreign Ministry Agnes Adlino Orifa Oswaha and Sudan’s ambassador to Juba, Essam Karar, discuss the attack on the Naam market in Abyei, October 19. Courtesy: The South Sudanese Foreign Ministry via Facebook.




A drone strike carried out by the military on the Naam market in northern Abyei — the disputed border territory between South Sudan and Sudan’s RSF-held West Kordofan — on Monday has stoked new diplomatic friction between Khartoum and Juba.




The death toll from the strike has risen to more than 150, as efforts to recover bodies were initially hampered by fires spreading from fuel depots hit in the attack, a South Sudanese source in the office of 

Yohana Akol Ngor

, the caretaker information minister in the Abyei administration, told Mada Masr.

 Around 8,000 people have also been displaced, the source said.




Juba responded by 

summoning 

Sudan’s ambassador to Juba, 

Essam Karar

, on the same day to protest the attack, a source at the South Sudanese Foreign Ministry told Mada Masr.

 

The ministry’s 

Undersecretary Agnes Adlino Orifa Oswaha

 told the ambassador that the strike was a dangerous development that called for urgent measures to prevent its recurrence and protect civilians, the source said.




The Sudanese military itself issued no immediate response. 

Days after the attack, in the early hours of Friday, Sudan’s Foreign Ministry 

issued

 a statement expressing regret over the casualties and categorically denying the military’s responsibility for it, calling the strike “similar to the crimes the rebel militia continues to commit.”




Yet a senior source in the Sudanese Armed Forces’ General Staff said the military had targeted fuel trucks arriving from South Sudan that he said were bound for the RSF. The source denied that civilians had been targeted, claiming that those killed were RSF members and that the strikes hit the group’s trucks at locations “outside the market, rather than the market as a whole.”




On Tuesday, residents and civil society activists took to the streets in Abyei to protest the bombing and demand protection for civilians, a source in local civil society organizations told Mada Masr.




Bulabek Deng Kual, the chief of the Ngok Dinka, 

one of the two main tribal groups in the area alongside the 

Messiria

, also urged the United Nations, the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development and the South Sudanese government to act to protect residents, the source said.




UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres 

condemned

 the attack in a statement issued late Tuesday. The toll, he said, is expected to rise as the UN interim security force in the region continues to verify casualties, with many missing. 




“I call on the governments of South Sudan and Sudan to take all steps possible to help prevent further attacks and uphold Abyei’s demilitarized status,” he added.




The strike hit a market that serves as an economic lifeline for communities in the region. 

Cross-border trade has made the 

Naam 

market a major source of income for the 

Ngok Dinka and Messiria

, 

a source in the Messiria

 previously told Mada Masr.

 The market is under RSF control, as is the rest of West Kordofan, and the group has used it to secure fuel supplies and as a staging and mobilization point for South Sudanese fighters recruited to fight alongside its forces, the source said.




The market sits in a region where the political dispute has never been settled. 

The 

2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement 

established special arrangements for Abyei and called for a referendum on whether the territory should belong to Sudan or South Sudan.

 The vote has never happened, and South Sudan’s independence in 2011 left the question of sovereignty unresolved. The 

UN Interim Security Force for Abyei 

remains responsible for security in the area. 




That unresolved status has long made Abyei vulnerable to tensions between the two countries, particularly as people, goods and armed groups move across a border that remains politically contested.




The dispute has been reignited as South Sudan prepares for its first general election in December. 

Juba’s decision in June to include Abyei among its electoral 

constituencies

 angered Khartoum, prompting regional diplomatic efforts to contain the fallout and keep the dispute from undermining the electoral process.




Meanwhile, Sudan has begun 

reorganizing

 its own approach to the issue. 

In early October, Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair and military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan appointed retired 

Major General Al-Khair Abu Mureidat

 to lead the Sudanese side of the joint oversight committee for Abyei, replacing Lieutenant General of Police Hamed Manan.




Abu Mureidat told Mada Masr that the committee would return to the agreements signed by the two countries and “pursue a peaceful resolution to differences.” He nevertheless reaffirmed Khartoum’s position that Abyei belongs to Sudan.




On October 15, Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin 

Salem

 

chaired 

the first meeting of Sudan’s national negotiating team on Abyei, which was established under a decision issued by Burhan in late September.




In remarks broadcast on Sudan’s national radio, 

Salem 

said the team would seek to restart talks with South Sudan on the region’s administration, security arrangements and final status.

 

The negotiations are to be based on the 2005 Abyei protocol and the

 2011 

Agreement 

on Temporary Arrangements for the Administration and Security of the Abyei Area.




***




RSF drones kill dozens at 

gold mine market

 in South Kordofan




Aftermath of an RSF drone attack on the market at the Bajon gold mine in Gadir, eastern South Kordofan, October 16. Courtesy: The Sudanese Mineral Resources Company via Facebook.




At least 45 people were killed and dozens injured when RSF drones hit the market at the Bajon gold mine in the military-held Gadir locality, eastern South Kordofan, on October 16, a medical source in the area told Mada Masr.




It was the second time in less than a week that drones had struck the mine. An earlier attack on October 10 caused no deaths, two miners in the area told Mada Masr.




The latest strike, however, hit a market where miners, traders and other workers depend on gold production for their livelihood. The attack destroyed processing facilities and nearby shops, putting hundreds at risk of losing their livelihoods in an area with few economic alternatives and limited relief services, they added.




The two miners blamed the RSF for the attack, as did the 

Sudanese Mineral Resources Company, 

which buys gold from traditional miners in 

Bajon.




In a 

statement 

issued on Saturday, the company said preliminary assessments showed damage to four major complexes housing gold extraction and processing 

mills 

but did not mention any casualties.

 It said fewer workers were likely to have been present because the attack took place on a Friday.




But the market was busy when the drones hit, according to a source close to miners and the families of those killed. 

The drones struck the main market and water-based processing 

mills

 in successive attacks, setting off fires that spread to nearby shops and storage areas.

 

Miners, laborers, shopkeepers and 

people providing services to the mining trade 

were among those caught in the strikes, the source said.




The death toll became clearer as rescuers pulled victims from beneath the rubble, according to the medical source who is in the local casualty-counting committees in Gadir. Reaching the site was difficult, while disrupted communications networks slowed both evacuations and the exchange of information between rescue teams, they said.




The full toll remains uncertain. 

No final list of casualties has been compiled, and a detailed breakdown by age 

or

 gender is not yet available, the medical source said.




Residents and local relief groups have been doing much of the work of transporting the wounded to medical facilities, he added. 

Using 

makeshift means

, they transported the injured to health facilities in Gadir, 

Liri and Talody,

 where shortages of medical supplies and limited capacity have made treatment difficult.

 Those needing emergency surgery or transfer to better-equipped hospitals face particular risks, the source said.




Families are also struggling to establish what happened to their relatives. Local volunteers have been burying the dead and trying to identify them, but many of the mine workers came from other parts of Sudan, he added. 

Due to unreliable communication networks,

 contacting families and verifying reports of deaths, injuries and missing people has been difficult.




Traditional mining sites attract workers from across Sudan and support a wider network of traders, transporters, equipment suppliers and businesses providing food and other essentials. Damage to facilities at Bajon threatens the livelihoods of people who depend on this trade, even if they were not directly involved in mining, the source added.




A South Kordofan government official informed of developments on the ground told Mada Masr that the attack took place in an area where mining operations, trade routes and contested zones of military control overlap, drawing traditional gold production into the war’s economic and logistical 

networks

.

 In his view, the RSF regard mining areas as strategically important because of their links to gold revenues and local trade.




Production at Bajon could remain disrupted until the damage to its processing facilities is assessed and repaired. 

Machinery, power supplies and other operating infrastructure may all affect how soon work can resume, a source informed of the 

Sudanese Mineral Resources Company

’s operations told Mada Masr.




The company is coordinating with technical teams and regional offices to assess the damage and determine its implications for production and gold deliveries in the state, an official in its environment and safety department said.




***




Dayslong m

ilitary drone strikes on Nyala




Nyala, the capital of South Darfur State, was pounded by military drones this week in one of the largest 

air campaigns against the seat of 

the RSF-led parallel administration in months.




The raids began on Friday, October 16, with strikes a military source described as among the most intense in months. They hit several sites, including the livestock market north of the city, where the source said RSF armored vehicles were targeted, and the Cinema neighborhood, where a training camp the RSF had set up inside Nyala University was hit.




The Tasis alliance 

said 

in a statement that the strike on the busy market killed at least 30 civilians and injured 43 others, claiming the drone was launched from the Egyptian military base in 

East Oweinat.




Meanwhile, the military 

said 

its air force carried out “concentrated” strikes that day on RSF command centers and the positions of what it called the group’s mercenaries in Nyala, killing dozens of them and destroying the command centers.




After a brief pause, the raids resumed on Sunday and continued until Wednesday. The strikes hit ammunition depots and the headquarters of RSF field commanders, the military source and a resident of the city told Mada Masr. Civilians were among those killed and injured, they added.




***




RSF drones hit Khartoum, airport area bears the brunt




Mere days after military drones began raiding the RSF’s de facto capital, the paramilitary group’s drones struck Khartoum in waves, 

concentrated

 around the international airport and extending across other parts of the capital’s south and east.




Three eyewitnesses told Mada Masr that explosions began in eastern Khartoum at around 6:30 am on Monday and continued in five waves throughout the day and evening. Military anti-aircraft fire could also be heard, they said.




Two drones fell in the Burri and Imtidad Nasser neighborhoods east of the airport in central Khartoum, killing four people, including three children from the same family, an official told Mada Masr. Their mother sustained serious injuries and was taken to the hospital, while parts of the family’s house were destroyed.




The drones had crossed eastern and northern Gezira State before some were seen flying over Khartoum’s East Nile locality toward the eastern part of the capital, a military source told Mada Masr. 

Monitoring systems suggested they were most likely launched from sites in the South Sudanese town of Rank and the Ethiopian cities of Bahir Dar in the Amhara region, and Asosa in 

Benishangul-Gumuz

, the source said.




On Wednesday, ground defenses shot down three drones, one in 

Bagir

 in southern Khartoum and two in East Nile, the military source added.




The area around Khartoum International Airport was among the main targets of the attacks. The airport, which had served as a major RSF stronghold during most of the war and witnessed some of the capital’s fiercest battles, reopened in February for the first time since the war began in April 2023.




In May, just a week after international flights resumed, drone strikes hit the airport. Khartoum publicly attributed the attack to Ethiopia, setting off a diplomatic rift that has since widened.




While the May attack damaged airport facilities and the runway, an engineer working at the airport told Mada Masr that this week’s attacks caused no damage.




Amgad Farid, Burhan’s political advisor, 

said 

on Monday that the airport continues to operate normally despite what he described as “terrorist attacks launched from some neighboring countries.”




***




RSF drone strike on White Nile’s 

Tendelti 

substation cuts power to North Kordofan cities




Two missiles from an RSF strategic drone set the power substation in Tendelti, White Nile State, ablaze in the early hours of Tuesday, knocking it out of service, a military source told Mada Masr.




The station feeds the main power line to North Kordofan State, so the strike cut electricity to three cities, Um Rawaba, 

Rahad

 and t

he state capital of Obeid,

 along with a number of villages and towns, an activist in Um Rawaba told Mada Masr.




Power 

resumed

 to North Kordofan on Wednesday evening once the state electricity distribution company had repaired 

the grid

, an official at the company said.

 Tendelti itself remains in total darkness, and restoring its transformer and power supply could take until the middle of next week, he added.




The blackout is 

disrupting

 other services, with water and bread shortages 

emerging

 in Tendelti, the activist said, warning that conditions will deteriorate if the outage drags on.




***




Dozens killed in a military drone attack on West Kordofan town




A military drone strike on the town of 

Dibab

 in West Kordofan State killed 84 people and wounded others on Sunday, a medical source in the area told Mada Masr, as conflicting accounts emerged over whether the attack hit civilians traveling or RSF fighters being moved toward the frontlines.




Three former West Kordofan government employees living in Muglad and aligned with the RSF told Mada Masr that the drones struck trucks carrying civilians traveling around the area.




However, an activist from the region said the strikes hit RSF fighters who had been mobilized and were on their way to Nyala before heading to the frontlines.




The men had been gathered under the supervision of RSF commander Adam Gareh and assembled in buildings previously used by the group’s security service, the activist said. They were later transferred in two transport trucks accompanied by several combat vehicles.




Videos circulated by activists on social media showed moments before the trucks were hit, along with the names of those killed.




The Tasis alliance, meanwhile, described the gathering as civilian. In a 

statement

, it said those targeted had 

congregated

 after attending a funeral and were preparing to travel by truck. According to the alliance, the drone first struck the truck, then returned to bomb people who had gathered to assist the wounded, leaving 80 dead and many more injured, including women and children.




Tasis added that the same drone struck 

Muglad,

 where it said a missile landed near a girls’ school and wounded at least two people.




The Emergency Lawyers rights group 

said 

military drones struck Muglad market on Saturday and resumed attacks on Dibab, killing dozens, including civilians.




The strikes took place as the military stepped up preparations for large-scale ground operations from North Kordofan into northern West Kordofan. Air raids on RSF positions have intensified across the region in recent weeks.




Throughout the past week, the air force carried out intensive strikes on West Kordofan’s Khawi, Abu Edam, Nayem, Um Maraheek, Udayyah and Babanusa, targeting RSF capabilities and supply lines, a military source in the Fifth Infantry Division in Obeid told Mada Masr.




***




RSF, SPLM-N

 press ahead with attacks

 on Blue Nile’s Kurmuk axis, military takes two areas in Geisan




Blue Nile’s Kurmuk locality has entered a second week of attacks by the RSF and SPLM-N forces led by Joseph Tuka, as the allies seek to advance from their positions toward military bases defending the state capital of Damazin.




Later in the week, the military mounted a surprise attack in the neighboring Geisan locality, taking two strategic areas that bolster its position on the eastern axis and 

could put RSF supply lines into the Wad al-Mahi areas they have recently seized at risk,

 according to a former military officer.




The latest round of fighting on the Kurmuk axis began on Monday at Baraka, a strategic military position 12 km northwest of the RSF-held town of Kurmuk. The RSF and SPLM-N forces set out from the town with dozens of combat vehicles and motorcycles, a military source told Mada Masr.




The attacking forces initially broke into Baraka, but the military regrouped and retook its positions, leading to fierce clashes that lasted all day and continued into Tuesday, the source said.




The two sides offered conflicting accounts of the outcome. 

The military’s Fourth Infantry Division in Damazin 

said 

on Monday that it repelled the attack, while the RSF announced on Tuesday that it took control of the position.




The situation on the ground remains unresolved, however, with both sides still present in the area and its outskirts, a second military source said. The source expected further decisive fighting in the coming days.




Baraka lies around 155 km from Damazin and is key to controlling southern Blue Nile. The military withdrew there in large numbers after losing Kurmuk to the RSF for a second time in mid-August.




The fighting spread to another key position on Tuesday, when the RSF and SPLM-N attacked Sali, which the military uses as a forward command post for operations in southern Blue Nile.




The allies opened with heavy artillery shelling and drone strikes before ground troops advanced from Sarkam, southeast of Sali, the first military source said. 

The 

attackers

 attempted to approach from two directions to encircle the position, with RSF units advancing from the southeast and Tuka’s forces from the south.

 Tuka’s fighters, however, failed to advance quickly enough to complete the maneuver, the source said.




Military reconnaissance aircraft had been tracking the advancing forces, allowing the military to exploit the delay and draw them into an ambush that killed more than 50 fighters, the source said. The military then searched the surrounding area and reinforced security positions around Sali, he added.




A former military officer said the attacks on Baraka and Sali form part of the RSF’s broader effort to increase pressure on Damazin. The military recognizes the strategic importance of both positions and is likely to use all available means to secure and defend them, he said.




On the Geisan front, the military launched a surprise assault at dawn on Thursday against RSF-held 

Bakori and Aklili

. Advancing from the north and east, its forces had taken full control of both areas by 10 am, seizing five combat vehicles and destroying others. 

The remaining RSF fighters in the area fled south toward the town of 

Geisan

, a third military source told Mada Masr.




The military later 

said 

it shot down a strategic drone near Bakori after tracking its entry into Sudanese airspace from Ethiopia.




Bakori, located around 70 km from Damazin, hosts the base of the Fourth Division’s 13th Infantry Brigade, which the RSF captured in August. Its recapture could pave the way for further military advances in eastern Blue Nile, the former military officer told Mada Masr, including toward Khartoum Beleil and the town of Geisan.




The gains would also give the military greater room to maneuver along the eastern axis and potentially cut RSF supply lines toward Minza al-Nimr and Jabal al-Namr in Wad al-Mahi locality, where the RSF made its first advances earlier this month, the officer said.




***




Tasis health minister leaves for Nairobi 

over

 Cabinet push to take control of medical aid




RSF-led Tasis government Health Minister Alaa Eddin Nugud inspects the progress of high school exams in Nyala, June 15. Courtesy: Tasis Health Ministry.




A fight over who gets to control healthcare resources and drug imports inside the RSF-led Tasis government in western Sudan has been simmering for months. Last week, it boiled over, sending Health Minister Alaa Eddin Nugud to Nairobi in protest.




The immediate trigger was a proposal by the Cabinet affairs minister to place international medical aid under the Cabinet’s control, which won Prime Minister 

Hassan 

al-

Taaishy

’s

 backing last week.

 

Taaishy is now treading carefully, trying to advance the proposal without pushing another member of the political leadership 

out of a government that is already sensitive to the cost of defections,

 officials in Tasis told Mada Masr.




The tussle for control over the portfolio is unfolding as health services across RSF-held areas in western Sudan

 continue to deteriorate

.

 Cities, villages and displacement camps sheltering hundreds of thousands of people face severe shortages. Funding cuts have forced many health centers to stop receiving international support, while the facilities that remain open are struggling to keep running. Many are also being pulled into the war effort, with medical resources and facilities needed for civilian care diverted to treat RSF fighters.




Nugud

 first raised the alarm around six months ago, when he complained of growing interference in his ministry’s affairs by the RSF’s medical department — a body closer to a military medical corps — and influential Tasis officials linked to the group, a Health Ministry official told Mada Masr.




At the heart of his objections, the official said, was what Nugud saw as an RSF effort to monopolize access to medicines and health facilities for the benefit of its members, interfering with the ministry’s ability to run the health sector.




Nugud threatened to resign, but Tasis officials stepped in to defuse the standoff, and he withdrew his resignation, a Cabinet official told Mada Masr.




But the protest came at a cost. The Cabinet official said Nugud subsequently faced tight restrictions on his movements and communications, as Tasis sought to prevent him from speaking to the media or leaving the government. With defections and departures threatening to undermine the administration, its leaders were wary of anything that might further damage its standing with international humanitarian organizations, whose procedural recognition is crucial to its ability to operate.




Around two months ago, the dispute took a new turn when Cabinet Affairs Minister 

Musa Khaddam 

put forward the proposal centralizing control over international aid for the health sector, the Cabinet official said.




Under the proposal, cash grants and in-kind donations would be routed through the Cabinet before reaching government departments, ending the direct arrangements between international organizations and the Health Ministry, the official explained.




Beneath the dispute over aid management there is also longer-running tensions over civilian drug imports, a Health Ministry official said. The RSF has traditionally controlled Indian pharmaceutical imports reaching Nyala through South Sudan and Uganda. 

When Tasis began establishing its own government, oversight of 

medicines for civilian use

 was handed to the Health Ministry.

 Influential RSF figures wanted that control back, along with the distribution contracts and profits that come with it, the official told Mada Masr.




The official warned that the new proposal could tip the balance in favor of those seeking to return civilian pharmaceutical imports to RSF control. Giving the Cabinet greater oversight of health resources, the official argued, would weaken the ministry’s position and allow influential RSF-aligned figures to sway the government into handing the imports back to the group.




The proposal remained idle until last week, when the government discussed the matter after months of delay and Taaishy voiced support for the plan, the official said.




Nugud pushed back, arguing that the plan would encroach on his ministry’s technical and executive remit and put decisions over health resources in the hands of the Cabinet, rather than those responsible for assessing the sector’s needs, a Health Ministry official said.




That was the breaking point, according to a source close to Nugud and another close to his family.




The minister suddenly went out of contact, prompting fears among his loved ones that he had been detained, the sources said. 

But he eventually got in touch to say he had arrived in Nairobi, where, they added, he would be safe from

 detention or restrictions.

 Both sources said he has continued to maintain political contacts with Tasis officials and members of his ministry.




With Nugud out of Nyala but not entirely out of the picture, Taaishy began to move forward. He issued directives to develop mechanisms and guidelines for transferring 

supervisory powers

 from the Health Ministry, a Tasis official said.




The government is keen to keep Nugud in his post and prevent the dispute from spiraling into a broader crisis, the official said. It is now looking for a formula that would clearly define the responsibilities of the Cabinet and the Health Ministry.




Taaishy’s stated aim is to centralize aid management, strengthen oversight and present Tasis to international partners and humanitarian organizations as a government capable of running public services. But shifting supervisory authority to the Cabinet risks limiting the ministry’s ability to assess its own needs and direct resources toward the health sector’s priorities, the alliance official said.




The stakes are particularly high in Darfur, where health facilities depend heavily on external supplies and humanitarian assistance. Clear procedures for receiving and distributing aid and ensuring the quality of medicines are essential to keeping services running, the official added.




For now, neither the Tasis official nor the Cabinet official has confirmed whether a final agreement was reached, and no binding executive decision has been issued.




***




Khartoum seeks UN-backed humanitarian steps to stave off 

truce pressure




Sudan’s military-led government is stepping up efforts to promote its vision for ending the war to Western capitals as pressure builds on it to respond to truce proposals advanced by the Washington-led Quad on Sudan.




To ease demands that it commit to a broader settlement, the government is seeking to show it can deliver on humanitarian issues as the war expands and conditions for civilians deteriorate, hoping that progress on aid deliveries and civilian protection would help curb international criticism, former and current Sudanese officials and sources close to Burhan and the TSC told Mada Masr.




Over the past week, Burhan sent letters to 

German Chancellor Friedric Merz

 and United States President Donald Trump, in what former officials said was an effort to project receptiveness to peace initiatives while holding firm on Khartoum’s demands to end the RSF’s presence.




That strategy would allow the government to demonstrate engagement on one front without being drawn into military and political arrangements it rejects, the sources said.




Khartoum is looking to the UN to help turn that distinction into a workable negotiating track, and to Western capitals to foot the bill for whatever is agreed upon.




Germany is one of the countries Khartoum is courting. 

Burhan’s letter to Merz was delivered to Berlin by Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi, who met German Foreign Office Minister of State 

Serap Guler

 on October 16.




Darfur’s centrality to the war and Minnawi’s standing as a key military ally informed his selection, according to a source at the Sudanese Embassy in Germany. The region is the RSF’s main sphere of influence and seat of its parallel administration, and has suffered some of the war’s worst humanitarian crises. 

Minnawi leads the Sudan Liberation Movement, a major military ally that, alongside the military establishment, has staunchly opposed any truce that would stop short of removing the RSF and its 

structures

 from Darfur.




According to the source, the government wants Berlin to help rally European support and revive commitments made at the 

International Conference on Sudan

 hosted by Germany in April, particularly those that could help fund and implement humanitarian measures through the UN.




The effort builds on Burhan’s discussions with the UN secretary general’s Personal Envoy Pekka Haavisto during the latter’s visit to Khartoum in September. The two discussed what a Foreign Ministry official said is referred to now within government circles as “confidence-building measures” — de-escalation, protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, unrestricted aid deliveries and the release and exchange of detainees. 




Sudanese authorities are now developing proposals to put those discussions into practice, with defined timelines and mechanisms for verifying compliance, a source close to Burhan told Mada Masr. These measures represent the area in which Sudan’s leadership believes progress remains possible at this stage, he added.




The government wants the UN to monitor implementation directly and help resolve obstacles as they arise, the source said. Each measure would have specific commitments and clearly identified international parties to carry them out, making it possible to measure progress without committing to a comprehensive agreement on a military truce, he added.




The outreach to Berlin is intended to help turn that framework into something workable, the embassy source said.




Days before the dispatch, German Ambassador to Sudan 

Philipp Vandel

 had 

met 

Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin 

Salem

 in Khartoum on October 12 to discuss bilateral relations, reconstruction and Germany’s contribution to addressing the war’s aftermath.




Minnawi gave the government’s public line at a 

meeting

 hosted by the Sudanese Embassy in Berlin on October 17 and attended by representatives of research centers, media outlets and humanitarian organizations.

 He said Khartoum was open to initiatives that respected Sudan’s sovereignty, but warned that a truce that fails to address the RSF’s deployment and armament would not bring lasting peace.




A day before Minnawi’s visit to Berlin, Burhan sent a letter to Trump “reaffirming Sudan’s commitment to US peace efforts,” the TSC chair and military chief 

wrote 

on X.

 Burhan said his government is ready “to work in good faith with all parties for a just, lasting peace that safeguards our sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and our people’s dignity.”




The pledge comes amid repeated clashes between Burhan and US Senior Advisor for African and Arab Affairs 

Massad

 Boulos over truce proposals advanced by the Quad he leads.

 Khartoum insists that the RSF withdraw from areas it occupies and disarm before any truce, while Boulos has increasingly urged the warring parties to accept the truce without preconditions.




The two sides have also clashed over US efforts at the UN Security Council to extend Darfur’s arms embargo to the rest of Sudan and enforce it against state institutions, a move Khartoum has strongly opposed on the grounds that it would equate the military with a “rebel militia.”




The direct appeal to Trump echoes Burhan’s earlier efforts to enlist the US president’s intervention outside Boulos’s negotiating track. 

In the aftermath of Fasher’s fall late last year, Burhan 

asked

 Saudi Crown Prince 

Mohammed

 bin Salman to urge Trump to intervene directly.




Khartoum is using its letters to Berlin and Washington, alongside contacts with the UN, to present itself as willing to engage with peace efforts in the face of international criticism over the continuing war and deteriorating humanitarian conditions, a former Foreign Ministry official and a former General Intelligence Service official said. At the same time, it is holding firm on its demands regarding the unity of state institutions and the future of the RSF, they added.




Sudan’s maneuvers come as international diplomacy over the war remains deadlocked, with a growing number of mediation initiatives, political tracks, truce proposals and humanitarian efforts yet to produce a breakthrough.




The UN Security Council’s October 16 open session on Sudan offered the same catalogue of concerns: the growing role of drone warfare, external support to the warring parties and an increasingly dire humanitarian crisis. Members remained divided over expanding sanctions, but expressed broader support for African-led mediation and coordination through the international Quintet.




Made up of the AU, UN, Arab League, European Union and IGAD, the Quintet has spent months trying to navigate rival political initiatives without throwing its weight behind any one of them. Its efforts to bridge the gap between Khartoum-sponsored intra-Sudanese dialogue and anti-war coalitions seeking their own political track in recent weeks have yet to prove feasible.




The latest attempt to coordinate international efforts came at the 

Sixth Consultative Meeting on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts in Sudan

, held in Geneva on Wednesday.

 The meeting brings together mediators to coordinate their approaches, with the Quad and Quintet expected to meet with Haavisto on its sidelines.




Meanwhile, the annual joint consultative meeting of the UN Security Council and the AU Peace and Security Council is scheduled for Friday.




A source at the AU Commission told Mada Masr that the bloc believes it should be possible for urgent humanitarian measures to proceed relatively independently of disputes over security arrangements and the political process, while remaining linked to both within a broader negotiating framework.




The proliferation of mediation forums remains a major obstacle to progress, the source added, particularly as Sudanese parties and international partners remain divided over the conditions for a truce and the future of transitional governance.

author: Omar Refaat
title: The caretakers
content:
Cairo – Summer 2025




Between the neck and the sword  




Yet, we go on, somehow, somewhen, somewhere. 




What’s making the unbearable bearable then? Who’s trying to make the fractured whole, the  paralysis somehow silently fruitful? Who’s trying to make the harshness of fate, hard not to adore and hard not to loathe fate, a feather more healthy? Who’s trying to reframe, to salvage, our maimed context on the run? 




Who, unsung, has been taking care of some of us in this beautiful brutal Cairo the past few, calamitous years? 




I looked around me and asked myself. 




What is love, in other words, and how is it being dispensed in the moonless waves of this incomprehensible grief?




What does love look like in the mutilated, public square now, mauled by this hellish, false reality shoved down our parched throats? What mermaid shapes is it taking in the fissures? In the plague of small, deranged men let loose on us, where does love drip, bloom calmly, lucidly, on its own? And we’re not even seeing it in the blur of our unfathomable resignation. Where do we, the afflicted of this earth, hold on, and who do we hold on to, hold dear, in this gale? What subtle kinds of repair are plugging the leak of meaning, the love-deficit, that won’t stop gushing with a grain of sand? Where is deliverance stealthily planting its seeds in abeyance, under the sign of this senseless darkness? 




Where are some of the unhailed glimmers of “capacious care” and “care commons,” the light river goddess of the drops of thankless sweat on which Capital, and State, are freeriding shamelessly, washing their hands of the very things which reproduce society on their behalf. 




And I have searched, dazed and yearning and lacerated, for the secret of heaven in the folds of this mortal coil, from mountaintops and through the gutter, and all I could find comes down to three things: love, beauty, art. 




Give us the holiest of trinities straight up in one go, and you are my savior, my friend. 




When the lab refuses capture 




How does urban space (which is shaped by political, economic, social, cultural forces operating in any given conjuncture and is never neutral or apolitical or absolute) refuse, intervene in, soar out of, the necropolis and kiss a thousand dancing stars back down upon the disquiet? How does it embrace difference and multiplicity and adversity and our glorious polyversality? Where is it trying to make the unconscious conscious, that misty bridge between the seen and the unseen and the yet-to-be-seen, experimenting with convivial ways of making life and sense and community, searching up the latent prospects of our intersubjective unfoldings and enfoldings on our own terms, new old tonalities of being and desiring and shaping and dreaming and self-forgetting together? 




Who are some of the people planning and improvising open-endedly, producing mini DIY sites of coping in the crannies of this evermore anguished, evermore giving, metropolis, carving times-out-of-time and spaces-out-of-space, commoning and instituting otherwise? 

Whose unpaid and/or severely devalued labor, physical, cognitive, immaterial, emotional labor, is keeping alive the alternative / independent art spaces and festivals and makeshift underground leftfield dancefloors in the heart of our crumbling city, those rare and endangered encounters and relational 

thinking and common feeling and mutual tending and collective looking and non-curricular, anti-canonical asking and radical study liminalities, 

against fiercely hostile conditions of near total defeat?

 Why and how are they doing this? How is the why inflecting their how?




What does it mean to nurse the jilted and the jaded, the leftovers, to smell a festering lesion and take responsibility for doing something about it? How do we not take this scarce bounty, this frail “right to the city,” right to unruly thought, right to marvel, right to fecund getting-together and, as obscene as it sounds, right to shared joy, that all-too-fleeting feeling of alignment with the cosmos, in this bleak for granted? How is it changing them, this kind of overspending of self? What are they prefiguring and foreshadowing, these “liminal blossoms” on the borders of joint becoming, those who toil for others to twinkle, for a chance for us to understand our interdependence, to discover untouched continents in each other’s eyes, to savor and have empathy for and be vulnerable, be immortal for a second, with each other, to soften our compromised craving and salvation, melt all this violence into gentleness? 




What’s the timbre of a caretaker’s cry for help? How to search for pathways and portals in the break and all those moral gates of no return?




That almost soundless sigh that we are here, not giving up on this failed and battered humanity. 




How is the world manhandling some of those who, inadvertently, end up protecting the sacred? How did it make them? What do we lose if we lose them? How are they surviving? What styles of being are they slicing up for us in the real? 




Who and what is all this for? 




What are we missing? Who is absent? Why not a Jacobin explosion actually and most urgently, right? Why this organic, rhizomic, insubordinate knowledge-making and sharing? How to swim against the tide of manufactured ignorance and cultural rot and structural blackmail and, last but not least, this pandemic of pettiness? 




The counter story, counter song. 




No one is an island, but only some are oases in this “affective abyss,” this spiritual drought we’re forced to scavenge. These implausible humans making my life, speaking for myself and many, many more, I’m sure, somehow silkier and more serious and lush. Those who’re doing the best they can, one mental meltdown, one soulbreak, one Sisyphean battle, one magnificent failure at a time, to make our plunge into the black hole of what comes next a little more thoughtful and a little more stirred, a touch more engaged, perhaps. Those are our people. 




Change one person’s view of reality, and you have altered the universe. 




Let’s borrow a lens from the Mahayana Buddhist path, the “wide vehicle” of freedom, according to that tradition, the way of sympathy and sanity, where the focus is no longer on individual liberation from Samsara, the wheel of suffering and sorrow and confused existence in the phenomenal realm, but on the liberation of all sentient beings, one by one; the Bodhisattva Vow, the most noble sentiment come forth from humankind. 




The bedrock of this school of thought and practice is helping, putting the other before the self, through loving-kindness and compassion and giving deed for all there is. Love, self-sacrifice, as the antidote to the wrenching pain of the illusion of separateness and the prison of consumption. Love as the only road to find at-one-ment. Love, done well, as the answer to the human predicament indeed. bell hooks, the black feminist social critic who saw love as an action, not a feeling, a verb, not a noun, wrote: “When we are loving we openly and honestly express care, affection, responsibility, respect, commitment, and trust.” Add to that list attention, exposed, undistracted attention, admiration too, and self-knowledge and self-mastery and selfless giving, and we have a pretty solid hold on the task at hand.




All the self-love, neoliberal mania soaking our manic-depressive screens: what’s radical love’s antidote to empire’s grand delusion? What is to be done, and how are we supposed to do it in our quaking?




Care. 




Care as worldview, as the awake side of being, as a slap in the face of artificial scarcity and depthlessness and the call to apathy and callousness and comprador order. Care as emotional and ethical mapping, as breaking coloniality at its marrow, as collective responsibility, the hidden freedom to make and remake ourselves and our values and symbols and imagination. Care as cultural reckoning, as libidinal opposition, as sign of contestation, as right agency, molding phoenix-selves out of the ashes of now. Care as political imagination and interdependence practice and what we do to maintain and remedy this pillaged and plundered planet, our will to continue pulsing on the verges.




Care as unfractured subjecthood, even if for just a filched moment here and there, as dignity supreme and community healing, as no-spectacle, as the cradle of quotidian transformation. Care as opening affective trails between disconnected lumps, as breaking false boundaries, as patching up the fragmentation of devotion and encounter, as escaping the panopticon, the thwarted potentialities, as wrestling with dominance in a smudged corner out of sight, smelling the roses along the way, fount and foundation of true orientation. Care as deterritorialization circuits that push against the logics of extraction and control, as value-making outside crude exchange and useless surplus. Care as actually existing anarchism, as safeguarding our rabidly assaulted hospitality and generosity. 




Care as what could’ve been and must be, the framework for how the world is grasped and handled, at every level of life. Care as inner integrity recognizing that only an other can help us save ourselves. Care as our friendliness and embrace toward the moment, as belief in the sanctity of the future. Care as resisting commodification and reification through collaboration and cooperation, what remains of our broken daydreams. 




To not be broken beyond fixing. To guard our ability to pay prayer to the pricelessness hiding in plain sight everywhere. To alter how we see and do the lack. To move, polyrhythmically, hushed in the cracks and shades, out of tune with the command. 




To make this reticent sky and all its mothers and fairies blossom stolen intimate conversations, drinking from and pollinating each other while everything around us is tearing us apart. To activate our common wounds into living webs that bind us. To know that you’re not out here alone, howling into the void, crying fetal in your bed whimpering what-have-we-done-to-deserve-this, that someone has taken the time and effort to make sure there’s a splash of color and promise and wonder and a stab at clarity-of-vision in our blackest days, for free mostly, a quiet politics of possibility, clawing out zones of ontological sovereignty in the walls of the collapsing cage. Art despite it all, with all its shame and glory and all its screams and whispers, when the gods don’t seem to be bearing witness. 




That some stranger, somewhere, has decided to give being-for-the-other a try. 




And guess what? It works. A snatched demo from an all-but-lost future, free from the ravages of uncare and inattention and erasure and avarice. 




To keep fighting, even if it’s already lost.




What is care to do in the midst of all this thrashing then, a butterfly adrift in a desert with no lake, so it doesn’t turn against itself and wither away, numb and bitter? 




Put differently, making common cause with the brokenness of being, planning without plan, creating improvised structures of care, learning and resistance, as Fred Moten and Stephano Harney write in their meditation on what they call the undercommons, the undercommons as a style of coming together, as lived epistemes, rooms of critique and refusal beyond disciplinary boundaries and supremacy’s logic. It is “fugitive sociality,” not playing along with the terms of belonging and relationality and alterity and subjecthood and recognition dictated by state and capital, other, already here, intentionalities of moving, gathering, feeling, learning, seeing, connecting, listening, exploring, studying within but against hegemonic systems. Transversal social formations within but against the present, that is, shared counter imaginaries and wishes, shards of wayward purpose, of momentary levity, glittering in the swamp.




Moten and Harney again: “In the undercommons of the social reproductive realm the means, which is to say the planners, are still part of the plan. And the plan is to invent the means in a common experience launched from any kitchen, any back porch, any basement, any hall, any park bench, any improvised party, every night. This ongoing experiment with the informal, carried out by and on the means of social reproduction, as the to come of the forms of life, is what we mean by planning; planning in the undercommons is not an activity, not fishing, or dancing or teaching or loving, but the ceaseless experiment with the futurial presence of the forms of life that make such activities possible. … Planning is self-sufficiency on the social level, and it reproduces in its experiment not just what it needs, life, but what it wants.”




To never lose the ability to imagine that things could be otherwise, even if they can’t or won’t. 




The micro tones of endurance. And if that’s all we’ve got for now, then let’s celebrate it. 




And then we look for those who will ride with us to the end of night, hold them close, set them free, take their pictures when they’re not looking, tell their tales to the angels when no one else is listening. Take care of them, love them well, fail them better. Make art, make verve, make splendor with them that reminds us, over and over and over till the end of time, that we’ve settled for far too little. Leave them every time as if there’s no tomorrow anymore.




These kinds of spaces, at their best, despite their inevitable flaws, teach us what it means to be human. 




They make flowers out of the crushed bits of us, lay some of the groundwork without which there’ll be no saving to be had. 




Why bother then, why fret with survival, no? 




Because there is tenderness, the finest rebellion, still in this orgy of cruelty. Because what we have lost can be turned into what sets us free.




When the old world is dying, and the new one struggles to be born, monsters come out, as Gramsci, that sweet Sardinian prophet, taught us. 




So thank you to all the cultural caretakers we talked to in this series, who have graced us in our darkest hours, and to the many, many more incredible humans doing this sort of hosting whom we were not able to talk to here. 




Thank you for breathing some light into the boundless pain in our hearts.  




Thank you for the beautiful forevers.

title: ‘Citizens’ health’ session at Egypt Forum 2026 boasts spending success with no mention of declining hospital bed numbers
content:
On Tuesday, the second day of Egypt Forum 2026, Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar described the political leadership’s support for the healthcare sector as unprecedented.




Speaking at the “citizen’s health” 

session

 of Egypt Forum 2026, he said the approach dated back to the beginning of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s presidency in 2014, when, he 

said,

 Egypt faced a massive “disease burden,” with a lack of data and years of inadequate budget allocations that had failed to meet developmental ambitions for the system, particularly as population growth accelerated.




The minister said the state’s development plan had delivered gains in the sector, citing 16 presidential initiatives that had benefited 95 million citizens at a cost of LE44 billion. 




Abdel Ghaffar stressed that success in healthcare should not be measured by spending levels, but by the results citizens ultimately experience.




Mada Masr looked into some of those results, drawing from government 

data

 published by the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).




One clear result over the time period is the notable decline in the number of beds in public hospitals between 2013 and 2024, with a drop from around 98,291 to 84,225. 




Over the same period, the number of beds in private hospitals rose from 26,009 to 36,014. 




Still, the combined total of beds in public and private hospitals fell from 124,300 in 2013 to 120,239 in 2024.




While Abdel Ghaffar portrayed inadequate budget allocations as a problem of the past, the state 

has consistently fallen short

 of the constitutionally mandated minimum for healthcare spending.

 Article 18 of the Constitution requires the state to allocate at least three percent of gross national product to public healthcare starting in FY 2016/17 and gradually increase spending over time. The state has not met this threshold since the Constitution was adopted in 2014. Since then, healthcare spending has not exceeded 1.7 percent of GNP in most years.




The government allocated 1.51 percent of GNP to healthcare in the current fiscal year’s budget, half the constitutional minimum. 




Meanwhile, the government has 

introduced

 a different method for calculating budget allocations that allows it to claim it is meeting the minimum spending threshold.

 




Rather than using its previous classification, which was based on the Health Ministry’s expenditure, the government now uses a “broader and more comprehensive” definition. Under this new definition, healthcare expenditure also encompasses spending by a number of off-budget economic authorities and companies as well as “any other entities providing healthcare services, such as police and military hospitals, Al-Azhar hospitals, the comprehensive health insurance system and its associated programs,” a Finance Ministry source previously told Mada Masr. Without publicly available data on these entities’ healthcare spending, it is impossible to verify whether they bring total annual healthcare spending to the constitutionally mandated minimum.




The same expansion of what constitutes annual “health spending” also allows the government to include the budgetary allocation for these entities’ debt repayments as investment in the sector, according to the same source.




The president 

confessed

 three years ago that the state is not meeting the constitutional requirements, saying in a public address that “the required numbers aren’t available, folks.”

 His comment came days after the government’s assertion that it was meeting the required spending levels.




Aside from its commentary on expenditure, the government’s Egypt Forum 2026 also highlighted the Universal Health Insurance System, one of the leading presidential health initiatives.




Egypt’s Healthcare Authority head, Ahmed al-Sobky, 

described

 the system as a comprehensive reform of Egypt’s healthcare sector, capping an “enormous leap forward” under Sisi, following earlier historic transformations under King Fouad I and former President Gamal Abdel Nasser.




Shortly before the forum, the government began promoting the second phase of the Universal Health Insurance System, launching a pilot phase in Minya Governorate. 




The first phase launch in the governorates of Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan began in 2018 and was 

completed

 in 2025.

 




Sobky said the system had achieved its objectives by strengthening social justice and reducing poverty by lowering out-of-pocket healthcare costs. He also cited the authority’s success in automating and digitizing services to improve speed and quality.




However, these statements overlook the 

issues

 that have plagued implementation in the six governorates covered by the first phase, most notably the severe shortages of numerous medications and the accumulation of insurance contribution arrears.

 In some cases, patients have been denied access to their medication due to overdue premiums. 




Such obstacles have led some beneficiaries to try to circumvent these barriers by changing their registered place of residence, drawing up new rental contracts in governorates where the system has not yet been implemented.




Unified Procurement Authority head Hesham Steit commented during Tuesday’s session on the importance of centralizing the procurement of medicines and medical supplies for different healthcare providers, saying it would ensure appropriate quality standards at the best prices.




But market shortages have only worsened since the authority’s establishment in 

2019

, manifesting most recently in 

severe shortages

 of several essential medicines and medical supplies in hospitals that accept the government’s health insurance.

 




Disputes with pharmaceutical and medical supply companies have left the authority with over LE40 billion in overdue payments to suppliers.

title: Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah referred to trial on charges of running unlicensed website
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was referred to trial on Thursday on charges of establishing and managing a website without a license, according to lawyer Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr’s legal counsel.




The Supreme State Security Prosecution referred Attalah to trial at a New Cairo misdemeanors court, where sessions will begin on October 27.




The referral decision came after Attallah was questioned for over six hours by prosecutors on Wednesday at the Supreme State Security Prosecution headquarters in New Cairo. Prosecutors questioned her during the session on charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news with the aim of disturbing public peace, with the latter accusation dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.




Azhari described the “haste” in the trial referral, which came just hours after the interrogation closed, and its scheduling for the coming week as “unjustified urgency” given the absence of circumstances in the case that require rapid resolution.




Wednesday’s investigation, labelled Supreme State Security Prosecution Case 9072/26, comprised information and documents compiled by the National Security Agency, including a report Mada Masr published earlier this month describing a 

wave of protests in prisons after the postponement of the criminal procedures law

, as well as a letter from the Supreme Media Regul

title: Israeli forces arrest cancer patient, daughter returning to Gaza
content:
Israeli forces arrested two Palestinians on Tuesday evening as they were returning home to the Gaza Strip after traveling to Egypt for medical treatment, according to a statement from their family and one of their relatives who spoke to Mada Masr.




The two arrested, a cancer patient and her daughter, were among patients who were traveling both in and out of Gaza via the Rafah border crossing, which was reopened on Tuesday for the first time following its extended three-week closure by Occupation 

forces

.

 




Twenty-nine patients, along with 42 companions, 

left

 the Gaza Strip on Tuesday to receive treatment in Egyptian hospitals. Among them were critical cases, chronic disease patients and those with serious injuries. 

A group of 75 Palestinians returning to Gaza after receiving medical treatment abroad arrived via Rafah the same day to 

the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.




The Rafah crossing, which was closed for almost two years after Israel 

occupied

 the crossing area in 2024, was 

reopened

 in February to provide passage to the sick and injured exiting Gaza for medical treatment, those returning from Egypt after completing treatment courses abroad, as well as for Palestinians who were 

stranded

 outside the strip and unable to return home amid Israel’s genocidal war.




Before they are allowed to return home, returnees must pass through extensive security checks administered by Israeli forces manning the Karam Abu Salem checkpoint. So far, a number of returnees have been subject to arrest at the site.




Amal Ghazy al-Rify and her daughter Yasmin Rifaat al-Rify were returning to Gaza on Tuesday after around two years of medical treatment in Egypt, according to 

Haitham al-Rify, a relative of the two women who lives in Gaza.

 Rify told Mada Masr that Amal is an elderly woman who was receiving treatment for her cancer, and that her daughter had traveled with her as a companion.




They decided to return without completing the medical course as Amal’s health and psychological condition had begun to deteriorate, he said, recalling that she had expressed her desire to return to Gaza despite her illness. “Before she set off on her way back, she said ‘I feel like I’m going to die, and I want to return to die in my country,” he recalled.




Describing Amal’s condition as critical, Rify said that she and her daughter had registered their data at the Palestinian Embassy in Cairo in order to return home, and that they had received prior approval for their travel. 




He condemned their arrest at the Karam Abu Salem checkpoint, stressing that neither is involved in any political or military activities. 




He told Mada Masr that the family was not informed by any entity about the circumstances of their arrest or their place of detention, adding that they have reached out to the International Committee of the Red Cross for further information but are yet to receive further details.




The family 

appealed

 in a statement on Wednesday to responsible parties, human rights and humanitarian organizations to intervene urgently to 

uncover the fate of Amal and Yasmine, to ensure their safety and work toward their release.

 




The two women left Gaza “seeking treatment and hoping for recovery and returned to find themselves facing detention instead of enjoying safety and stability after a tough medical trip,” according to the family’s statement, which added that medical “treatment is a right, dignity is a right and freedom is a right that cannot be infringed upon without a legal justification.”




The pair are not the first to be arrested during their return journey back. Before the extended closure of the crossing through October, Occupation forces arrested a young man named Mohamed Jihad al-Shourbajy at the border, prompting the Palestinian Center for the Defense of Prisoners to warn that the crossing was becoming a “trap” for Palestinians returning to their families. 




At the time, the center 

questioned

 the role of the European mission stationed at the crossing and its responsibility for ensuring the safety of citizens transiting through it.

 




Amal and Yasmin have not been allowed to contact their lawyers, the center stated on Thursday, expressing concern about their safety and conditions in custody. It added that their arrest brings the total number of Palestinians arrested at the crossing to seven, stressing that the border has come to represent a risk to travelers and again questioning the role of the European Union delegation at the facility.




The European mission has been in place in a technical capacity at the Rafah crossing since its February reopening. They suspended their work half-way through March in protest at another case of arrest. The mission described the March incident as a clear violation of the agreements signed by the parties regulating the crossing’s functioning and ensuring travelers’ freedom of movement.




When the crossing opened for two-way traffic in February, Palestinians returning to Gaza were subject to inspections at “Regevim,” a newly established Israeli-run checkpoint several kilometers inside the crossing in Palestinian Rafah. 




Palestinians subjected to these inspections 

described

 them to Mada Masr at the time as “humiliating and degrading,” explaining that they were blindfolded, restrained and interrogated for hours before being allowed to pass.




In July, the Occupation moved the checkpoint to Karam Abu Salem, in the strip’s southeast, continuing its inspections there. People returning to Gaza are required to navigate the Rafah crossing, travelling around 50 km east to the checkpoint, before they are finally allowed to enter the strip fully.




Israel’s Public Broadcasting Corporation, Kan, cited unnamed sources in July to claim that the move came after the discovery of attempts to smuggle unauthorized goods into the strip, including cigarettes, tobacco and electronic equipment. It claimed that the move would not hinder travelers’ movement and that the checkpoint’s relocation was to improve inspections and ensure the safe and efficient continuation of the crossing’s operation.




Regardless, the Occupation has repeatedly closed the crossing, as indicated in a 

report

 on border activity in September issued by the Gaza Crossings and Borders Authority.

 Severe disruptions  to movement were evident as the crossing was closed for 20 out of 30 days in the month. 




Zaher al-Wahidy, information unit manager at the Gaza Health Ministry, said around 30 to 40 patients are able to travel on days when the crossing is open; a tiny fraction of the 21,000 patients, of whom 5,600 are children, who have completed the necessary documents for medical transfer and are waiting inside the strip. 




Ten patients referred for treatment abroad died during the extended three-week closure as they were not able to travel, Wahidy said, adding that “every day of delay could cost the lives of more patients.”




He estimated that around 2,000 patients have died so far as a result of being prevented from traveling for treatment since Israel 

took control of the Rafah crossing 

in May 2024.




The Health Ministry in Gaza said last week that the crossing’s closure has led to a severe and rapid accumulation of critical medical cases, as waiting lists grow daily, exceeding the capacities of the exhausted and besieged hospitals’ ability to accommodate or provide the minimum standard of treatment. 




The ministry has 

called

 for serious and urgent pressure on Israel to open the strip’s crossings and facilitate the exit of patients in critical condition to save whoever can be saved.




Wahidy also emphasised that at least 200 patients should be allowed to travel every day, a step he said would help bring down the medical transfer waiting lists to which tens of people are added daily.




With hospitals and medical facilities decimated, and access to equipment and supplies 

limited

 by Israeli obstruction of the passage of goods into Gaza, options for treatment inside the strip are severely limited.




There is a “total absence of chemotherapy capacity,” Wahidy said, noting that equipment for surgeries is also limited since there is low capacity for diagnostic services through MRI scanning.




The Gaza Health Ministry 

warned

 on Thursday that limited access to engine oils is threatening hospital operations, which rely primarily on generators, currently at critical risk of “forced and sudden shutdown.”

content:
It took four days of successive presidential reiterations before the various parties began to grasp that, this time, it is different.




And no wonder. Never in Egypt’s modern history has the head of state chosen to hand power over voluntarily. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi himself

That’s why when the president opened his speech at the Armed Forces’ educational seminar on Wednesday by announcing he would not extend his rule, the confusion was plain on all sides, state institutions included.




At the seminar, Sisi said he had no intention of amending the Constitution. The audience hesitated for a few seconds before applauding. And many people

.




The next day, he stated the announcement in clearer terms. But the statement, issued by the presidential spokesperson, was edited, changing “until 2030” into “until the last day of his rule.” There is a big difference between the two formulations. title: State security prosecution summons Mada Masr editor-in-chief for investigation
content:
Lina Attalah, Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief, received a summons today from the Supreme State Security Prosecution to attend a questioning session on Wednesday, October 21. The summons did not say why she is being questioned.




The new investigation, Case 9072/2026, is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr, its journalists and its editor-in-chief in the past six years. The most recent was in August 2025, when the security prosecution released Attalah on LE30,000 bail. She was questioned at the time on charges of “broadcasting false news” and “using a website without a license,” based on a National Security Agency investigation report, in relation to a Mada Masr story on prisoners’ complaints of abuse in detention facilities. 

When 

asked 

why she trusted the sources cited in the story, Attalah said she had abided by professional journalistic standards and had acted in the public interest.

content:
Ihsan Yaghi’s house in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah is scorched from the inside. Piles of rubble fill the rooms she and her husband walk through to see what remains. What was not demolished by nearby Israeli strikes has been blackened by fire, with soot covering the interior walls. But Yaghi refuses to leave.




“Despite everything, this is still my land, and we have a very strong attachment to this land that we can’t let go of,” Yaghi tells Mada Masr.




Yaghi’s is one of roughly 100 families that have, since July, returned to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, one of around 70 villages in southern Lebanon still under Israeli occupation, its residents displaced, its homes destroyed, its fields unreachable. The question of what should be done for the south, how to rebuild and how to return people to their land under continued occupation, has become one of the most pressing political questions in Lebanon. The answer currently on offer from the Lebanese government and its international partners is the “pilot zone.”




On July 21, the United States announced 

the official commencement

 of pilot zone operations in three villages in southern Lebanon: Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiyah. content:

In her exhibition, Z for Zarafa, which opened at Gypsum Gallery at the start of June and closed on September 23, Lara Baladi takes us through a scavenger hunt of moments, leading us into an archive of revolution, specifically looked at from an aftermath vantage point of movement, migration, displacement and the ultimate wrestling for freedom.




The exhibition acts as a physical installation of aspects of an online database, 

Anatomy of Revolution

consolidates

content:

content:

title: State security prosecution releases journalist Rasha Azab on LE10,000 bail
content:
Journalist Rasha Azab was released on LE10,000 bail on Monday evening by the Supreme State Security Prosecution following questioning in relation to a tweet she published in recent weeks regarding the conduct of the Interior Ministry and its impact on the public mood. 




She was questioned on charges of “promoting the perpetration of terrorist acts” and using a website to promote ideas calling for doing so in Supreme State Security Prosecution Case 8025/2026, her defense lawyer, Ragia Omran, told Mada Masr. 




Azab was questioned on her reasons for publishing a tweet, in which she wrote, on September 23, “how long does it take to go from ‘the Interior Ministry are thugs’ to ‘the people want the fall of the regime.’” Azab responded that her tweet was commentary on the case of Dina Ezzat, a woman who called for her husband’s release on social media in September, after he was arrested from their Nasr City home by authorities in their local area. content:
Journalist Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emaira has been issued a 15-day detention order by the Supreme State Security Prosecution, Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights lawyer Islam Salama told Mada Masr.




Abu Emaira was presented before prosecutors for the first time at 10 pm on Saturday night, five days after security authorities launched an arrest campaign targeting him and five of his colleagues from the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh.




The whereabouts of the other five Matsda2sh journalists are still unknown as of time of publishing.




Salama told Mada Masr he attended with Abu Emaira the investigation session which began at 10 pm on Saturday evening and continued for over 10 hours. content:
Dozens of journalists participated on Saturday in a symbolic sit-in inside the Journalists Syndicate to call for the release of the Matsda2sh journalists, whose whereabouts remain unknown after security forces launched an arrest campaign targeting six of the independent fact-checking platform’s staff on Monday.




While the sit-in was scheduled to end at 5 pm, several members of the syndicate’s general assembly announced that they would remain inside the syndicate, keeping the sit-in open-ended until the Matsda2sh journalists are released.




The syndicate’s board also announced that an emergency meeting would be convened on Monday with a single clause on the agenda: how to respond to the arrest of the six journalists.

title: Unconfirmed report asserts official detention order issued for Matsda2sh team amid security leaks, media accusations
content:
A report that emerged on Friday night has claimed that the Supreme State Security Prosecution issued a formal detention order on Thursday for the six journalists from the Matsda2sh editorial team who were arrested earlier in the week.  




The Al-Masry Al-Youm report described the issuance as ordering the journalists’ detention for 15 days.




But as no official announcement has been published by prosecuting authorities, lawyers and a Journalists Syndicate source speaking to Mada Masr cast doubt on the veracity of the news report’s claim, which represents the first indication of an official detention order since the journalists’ arrests. 




Security forces arrested and forcibly disappeared the six members of the Matsda2sh editorial team in the span of 24 hours in a campaign that was launched Monday night. No official statement on the arrest was published until Thursday.




None of the journalists have been presented formally before prosecuting authorities, EIPR lawyers told Mada Masr, and neither their families nor the Journalists Syndicate have been informed of their place of detention, the syndicate source confirmed.

title: How a war in Tigray could set off a more complex fight
content:
For much of the past year, tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region had been steadily escalating toward confrontation.




The threat for those in Tigray, as much as for those in the wider region, was that the area could tip back into the kind of war that devastated the state between 2020 and 2022, but, this time, with a supercharged regional dimension. Officials in Addis Ababa and Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, have traded increasingly hostile accusations as the peace established at Pretoria frayed, while intermittent clashes and drone strikes produced episodes of serious violence. 




From the sidelines, Eritrea, Egypt, Somalia and Sudan — a pragmatic, loosely aligned anti-Ethiopia coalition — looked on. Then, on September 20, a drone struck a truck carrying more than 41 tons of food aid for displaced people in northwestern Tigray, setting the vehicle and its cargo ablaze.

title: Drones target Addis Ababa military headquarters; Federal forces advance on Tigrayan capital
content:

At 6 am, Ethiopian defense systems detected a “simultaneous terrorist attack attempt using suicide drones targeting vital facilities within the capital,” the security source said. “The attack aimed to strike the military command headquarters in the Tor Hailoch area, as well as the vicinity of the 24th Infantry Division headquarters in the Kirkos district of central Addis Ababa.”

postponed

statement

title: Italian court sentences 3 Egyptian officers to jail in Regeni murder case
content:
An Italian court 

sentenced

 on Monday three Egyptian security officers to 10 years imprisonment in absentia for the 2016 kidnapping of Giulio Regeni.

 




The convicted officers are Major Magdy Sherif of the National Security Agency and police officers Colonel Ather Kamal and Colonel Hesham Helmy. 




The court dismissed the charge of 

conspiracy to commit aggravated murder

 that was leveled against Sherif, while another security official implicated in the case, 

Major General Tarek Saber, was acquitted of all charges.

 




The Italian prosecution had requested in its closing arguments a life sentence for Sherif and 17 years and six months for the three other defendants.




“A ruling issued in the name of the Italian people, a ruling that stands as a safeguard for all the Giulios and Giulias of the world,” said Alessandra Ballerini, the family’s lawyer. Ballerini added that the verdict proves that the body of evidence presented before the court withstood its scrutiny.




“From this evening on, all regimes, along with their apparatuses and agents, will be forced to remember that human dignity is inviolable, as are human bodies; that impunity can be defeated; and that democracies can put a stop to arbitrary abuse,” she added.
